newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil trade fears revive devaluation debate.
newsitem.headline: Brazil trade fears revive devaluation debate.

text.p: Fears over Brazil's mounting trade gap, which is expected to soar to record highs this year, has renewed calls for a speedier devaluation of the real currency.
The Central Bank depreciated the currency by about 7.0 percent against the dollar in 1996 and has signalled it will follow a similar strategy this year.

But critics say that without a faster depreciation, Brazil's 1997 trade deficit could rise beyond forecasts of $8.0 billion in 1997, which could put too much pressure on the current account and force Brasilia to slam its doors on imports.

"To avoid putting the economic opening and all of its successes at risk, it is necessary to return to real exchange rate depreciation," the National Development Bank (BNDES) recently advised in a 60-page report on the Brazilian economy.

The BNDES urged the Central Bank to depreciate the real at a faster rate than inflation to attain a real depreciation. It noted that last year, the currency actually appreciated in real terms because inflation stood at about 10 percent with a 6.9 percent currency devaluation.

The export community and other critics of the current exchange rate policy blame the strong real for Brazil's poor trade performance in 1996 and the bleak outlook for 1997. Brazil's 1996 trade gap, which should be announced this week, will likely come in at a record $5.0 billion, despite initial government forecasts for a balanced trade account.

Import growth has soared about 15 percent over the past six months on a moderate economic recovery, while exports shrunk by about 1.5 percent. Although the period is seasonally weak for exports, the fast pace of imports has surprised economists.

Brasilia has repeatedly said it is not worried by the worsening trade trend, noting that the gap is a natural consequence of greater economic opening. The government says the deficit can be easily financed with foreign direct investment and short-term capital flows. Brazil had racked up $60.4 billion in foreign reserves by November last year.

Also, the Central Bank has said it will not hold exchange rate policy hostage to trade issues and that export promotion should be achieved through tax breaks, low Also, the Central Bank has said it will not hold exchange rate policy hostage to trade issues and that export promotion should be achieved through tax breaks, lower port costs and other non-exchange mechanisms.
Still, the Central Bank in November began to slowly increase monthly depreciations of the real in what was widely viewed by the market as a reaction to the worsening trade numbers.

The real was depreciated by 0.58 percent in November and 0.63 percent in December, up from 0.55 percent in October. So far in January, the Central Bank has depreciated the real by 0.24 percent, reflecting a pace of decline similar to that in December.

But even with monthly depreciations of 0.60 percent, the real would close 1997 about 7.5 percent weaker against the dollar, which might not result in a real depreciation given inflation estimates of between seven percent and eight percent for the year.
And economists said there were key obstacles preventing the Central Bank from speeding devaluation faster than a monthly average of about 0.60 percent.

One is that in the absence of fiscal restraint, a strong real has helped bring inflation down to its lowest levels in 50 years. Even the BNDES warned that if there is no serious improvement in Brasilia's fiscal performance, a speedier depreciation of the real could reignite inflation.
Economists said a faster devaluation rate might also force the government to raise interest rates to keep dollars in the country.

"Nobody wants to see interest rates increasing, so it is a bit difficult to see something like even an eight percent depreciation over the year," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC bank in Brazil.
